title: Mega Man 2
japaneseTitle: ロックマン2 Dr.ワイリーの謎
shortDescription: Capcom's crowning 8-bit platforming achievement, celebrated for non-linear robot master selection, weapon-rock-paper-scissors mechanics, and Takashi Tateishi's immortal soundtrack.
historicalSignificance: Perfected the non-linear stage selection and weapon-absorption gameplay loop, becoming Capcom's best-selling NES title (1.5 million copies) and establishing Mega Man as an international icon.

editorialContent.overview: Produced on Capcom's internal free time by director Akira Kitamura and artist Keiji Inafune after the modest commercial sales of the 1987 original, Mega Man 2 (Rockman 2 in Japan) was an absolute passion project. Released on Christmas Eve 1988, it became a runaway global masterpiece that permanently defined action platforming on the Nintendo Entertainment System.
editorialContent.gameplayMechanics: Players guide the blue robotic hero Mega Man across eight non-linear stages governed by rogue Robot Masters: Metal Man, Air Man, Bubble Man, Quick Man, Crash Man, Flash Man, Heat Man, and Wood Man. Defeating each boss awards their signature weapon, creating a brilliant 'rock-paper-scissors' affinity matrix where each robot master is critically weak to another's armament.
editorialContent.technicalInnovation: Mega Man 2 squeezed remarkable graphical fidelity and tight 60fps responsiveness out of the NES, utilizing Capcom's MMC1 memory management mapper to eliminate sprite flicker while rendering towering mechanical bosses like the Dragon and Guts-Dozer across multi-screen scrolling arenas. Takashi Tateishi's driving electronic rock soundtrack, particularly the Dr. Wily Stage 1 theme, stands as one of the greatest musical compositions in video game history.
editorialContent.culturalImpact: With over 1.5 million physical copies sold, Mega Man 2 transformed Capcom into an elite global publisher and established Mega Man alongside Mario and Sonic as an enduring industry mascot.
editorialContent.preservationNotes: Preserved on authentic 256KB MMC1 cartridge ROM dumps. Emulation must strictly respect NES scanline sprite evaluation timing to preserve Capcom's intentional hit-pause feedback.
